label: Flexion-intolerant low back (disc-type pattern)
description: A low-back pain pattern that is provoked by lumbar flexion, especially loaded or sustained flexion and flexion under compression. Functionally this is the classic 'disc-type' / derangement presentation (e.g. disc bulge/herniation or flexion-sensitized tissue): pain increases with bending forward, slumped sitting, rounding the spine under load, and on repeated/sustained forward bending; it typically centralizes (eases, retreats toward the midline of the back) with extension or neutral-spine positioning. The person is usually most symptomatic in the morning and after prolonged sitting. The goal of routing is to load the trunk and hips while keeping the lumbar spine out of flexion and well-braced.
red_flags: pain, numbness, tingling or weakness radiating down the leg below the knee (suspected radiculopathy)
progressive or marked leg weakness / foot drop
saddle (groin/inner-thigh/perineal) numbness, or new bowel or bladder dysfunction — possible cauda equina, seek emergency care immediately
pain that is constant, unremitting, and worse at night or with rest
symptoms peripheralizing (spreading further down the leg) with activity rather than centralizing
intake_questions: Does bending forward, slumped sitting, or rounding your back under load make it worse, and does leaning back or standing tall ease it?
Is the pain only in your back, or does it travel into your buttock, thigh, or below the knee?
How long can you sit before it flares, and is it worst in the morning or after sitting?
Can you hip-hinge to a bodyweight deadlift / pick something off the floor with a neutral, braced spine without symptoms?
workaround: Favor neutral-to-slightly-extended spine and hip-dominant loading. Drill hip-hinge competency first (dowel-on-back, RDL pattern, hip-hinge to a box) so load goes through the hips, not a rounding lumbar spine. Keep all hinges, squats and rows in a braced neutral spine; raise the start position (rack pulls, trap-bar from blocks, elevated-handle work) to shorten the flexion range. Emphasize anti-flexion/anti-extension core endurance (dead bug, bird dog, Pallof, suitcase carry, plank progressions) over loaded crunch/sit-up patterns. Avoid loaded spinal flexion, deep/sustained forward bending, and early-morning heavy hinging. Teach the brace + hip-hinge before adding external load, and progress load only while symptoms stay central and don't travel down the leg.

label: Extension-intolerant low back (facet / stenosis pattern)
description: A low-back pain pattern provoked by lumbar extension and by sustained standing/walking, and eased by flexion or sitting. Functionally this is the facet-joint / lumbar (or foraminal) stenosis presentation: pain with arching back, overhead/standing-press postures, prolonged standing or walking, and end-range extension; relief with forward bending, sitting, or leaning on a support (the classic 'shopping-cart sign' in stenosis). The aim of routing is to keep the lumbar spine out of end-range extension and to control the extension that leaks in during pressing and overhead work via anti-extension bracing.
red_flags: leg pain, heaviness, numbness or weakness brought on by walking/standing and relieved by sitting or bending forward (neurogenic claudication) — needs evaluation
progressive leg weakness, foot drop, or worsening balance
saddle numbness or new bowel/bladder changes — possible cauda equina, seek emergency care immediately
bilateral leg symptoms
night pain that is constant and unrelated to position
intake_questions: Does arching back, reaching overhead, or standing/walking for a while make it worse, and does sitting or bending forward relieve it?
How long can you stand or walk before your back or legs flare?
Do you get leg heaviness, cramping, or numbness with walking that eases when you sit or lean forward?
Is the pain central in the back, or does it spread into the buttocks or legs?
workaround: Favor a slightly flexed or neutral lumbar spine and anti-extension control. Cue ribs-down / posterior pelvic tilt and a braced trunk so the lower back doesn't hyperextend, especially in pressing, overhead and hinge lockouts. Prefer supported and incline pressing (chest-supported, landmine, low-incline) over strict standing overhead pressing; if pressing overhead, use a half-kneeling or seated braced position to remove the standing lumbar-extension demand. Use anti-extension core work (dead bug, plank, ab-wheel within tolerance, hollow holds) to teach the person to resist arching. Trunk flexion-biased and hip-flexor mobility work, walking in slightly flexed/supported positions, and bike over treadmill are usually well tolerated. Avoid loaded lumbar hyperextension, hyperextension benches into end range, deep cobra/superman end-range, and prolonged unbroken standing under load.

label: Sacroiliac (SI) joint dysfunction / pain
description: Pain localized to one side of the low back / upper buttock around the dimple of the sacroiliac joint, often pointed to with one finger just below and medial to the back of the pelvis. Functionally it is provoked by asymmetrical, single-leg, and shear-loading tasks: stepping up, single-leg stance, rolling in bed, getting in/out of a car, transitioning sit-to-stand, and wide-stance or asymmetrical hinging/lunging. It is frequently associated with pregnancy/post-partum and with hypermobility, and can flare with both too much and too little load. Routing favors symmetrical, well-braced bilateral loading and building hip/glute and lateral-trunk control to stabilize the pelvis.
red_flags: bilateral or alternating buttock pain with morning stiffness lasting >30 min and improvement with exercise in a young adult (screen for inflammatory/axial spondyloarthritis) — refer out
fever, unexplained weight loss, or history of cancer with new pelvic/back pain
true progressive leg weakness or numbness, or bowel/bladder changes
pain following significant trauma (fall, collision) — rule out fracture before loading
rapidly worsening pain unresponsive to position change or relative rest
intake_questions: Can you point to the pain with one finger, and is it just to one side near the back dimple of your pelvis?
Do single-leg tasks (stairs, getting out of a car, rolling over in bed, standing on one leg) provoke it?
Are you currently or recently pregnant/post-partum, or generally very flexible/hypermobile?
Does symmetrical loading (e.g. two-leg work) feel more stable than single-leg or wide/asymmetrical positions?
workaround: Favor symmetrical, bilateral, well-braced loading and reduce shear across the pelvis. Prefer two-leg hinges/squats and bilateral or supported single-leg variants (split squat with rear-foot/hands support, narrow split stance) over wide lunges and uncontrolled single-leg jumps. Build the muscular 'corset' around the SI joint: glute med/max (hip thrust, bridges, banded abduction in pain-free range), and anti-rotation/anti-lateral-flexion trunk work (Pallof press, suitcase carry, side plank) to control pelvic shear. Keep stance narrower and avoid deep, asymmetrical, twisting, or end-range hip positions early. For hypermobile/post-partum presentations, prioritize stability and load tolerance over stretching the already-loose joint. Progress single-leg loading gradually once symmetrical work is symptom-free.

label: Lumbar erector / paraspinal muscular strain
description: An acute or subacute muscular strain of the lumbar erector spinae / paraspinals — the classic 'tweaked my back' from a heavy or awkward lift, often with sudden onset, muscle spasm/guarding, diffuse one- or two-sided low-back ache, and pain on contraction or stretch of the muscle. Functionally it is provoked by hinging and lifting under load, deep stretch into flexion, and trunk extension against resistance, and it is generally movement- and load-dependent rather than radiating into the leg. This is typically self-limiting and responds to graded reloading; routing protects the irritated tissue early, then rebuilds hinge tolerance and erector endurance.
red_flags: pain radiating below the knee, or new leg numbness/tingling/weakness (suggests nerve involvement, not just muscle)
saddle numbness or bowel/bladder changes — emergency
significant trauma mechanism, or inability to bear weight — rule out fracture
no improvement at all after ~2-4 weeks of sensible relative rest and graded loading, or progressive worsening
fever, night sweats, or constitutional symptoms with the back pain
intake_questions: Did it come on suddenly during a specific lift or movement, and is the pain in the muscle/back rather than shooting down the leg?
What movements or loads reproduce it right now (bending, lifting, twisting, standing up)?
Is there visible spasm/guarding, and does the back feel 'locked'?
How many days ago did it start, and is it improving day to day?
workaround: Early phase: avoid bed rest — keep gently moving and stay within a pain-tolerable range; use light, pain-free movement (walking, hip-hinge pattern unloaded, cat-camel, McGill 'big-3' style dead bug/bird dog/side-plank) to reduce guarding. Reload graded: rebuild the hip-hinge with a dowel and light load, keep a braced neutral spine, and progress trap-bar/RDL/rack-pull load as tolerance returns. Favor supported, bilateral, neutral-spine loading; temporarily reduce range and load on heavy deadlift/good-morning patterns and on loaded spinal flexion. Build erector and trunk endurance (back extensions to neutral, carries, isometric holds) rather than chasing range or stretch into the painful end. Avoid maximal/ballistic lifts, deep loaded flexion, and aggressive end-range stretching of the strained tissue until pain-free under submaximal load.

label: Quadratus lumborum (QL) strain / lateral low-back pain
description: Pain in the deep lateral low back, between the bottom rib and the top of the pelvis on one side, attributable to the quadratus lumborum. Functionally it is provoked by side-bending, single-arm/offset carrying and asymmetrical loading, hip-hiking, rotation, and prolonged static postures (e.g. sitting hitched to one side). It often presents with one-sided tightness, pain on lateral flexion toward and stretch away from the involved side, and difficulty straightening up from a bent position. Routing reduces asymmetrical lateral-flexion load early, then rebuilds frontal-plane (anti-lateral-flexion) trunk control.
red_flags: flank pain with fever, painful urination, or pain that is not movement-related (rule out kidney/visceral source) — refer out
pain radiating into the leg, or new leg numbness/weakness
constant night pain or constitutional symptoms (weight loss, fevers)
trauma mechanism with inability to load — rule out fracture
no response to graded loading and load management over several weeks
intake_questions: Is the pain in the side of your low back between your ribs and pelvis, on one side?
Do single-arm carries, side-bending, hip-hiking, or sitting leaning to one side provoke it?
Does it hurt to bend toward the painful side, or to stretch away from it?
Is the pain clearly movement-related (vs. present regardless of position, or with urinary symptoms)?
workaround: Reduce one-sided lateral-flexion stress early and rebalance the frontal plane. Temporarily favor symmetrical, two-arm or evenly-loaded carries over heavy single-arm/offset carries; keep the trunk stacked (ribs over pelvis) and avoid hip-hiking and prolonged side-leaning postures. Reintroduce frontal-plane control progressively: light suitcase carries, side planks within tolerance, anti-lateral-flexion holds, and Pallof/anti-rotation work to retrain the QL and obliques as stabilizers. Address contributing factors (leg-length/seating asymmetry, weak hip abductors). Avoid deep end-range side-bending stretch into pain, heavy asymmetrical loading, and ballistic rotation until the side is symptom-free under light symmetrical load. Progress toward loaded unilateral carries once tolerant.

label: Activity-specific lumbar/QL endurance fatigue (running impact)
description: A non-pathological, activity-specific limitation: the lumbar erectors and QL fatigue and tighten under repetitive impact and prolonged anti-extension/anti-lateral-flexion demand — most commonly the low-back tightening, aching, or 'pump' that builds during longer runs or repeated impact and resolves with rest. This is an endurance/capacity limit (trainable) rather than a pain pattern: there is no radiating or red-flag symptom, no specific injury event, and symptoms are predictable and load-dose dependent. Routing treats it as a conditioning target — build trunk endurance and the spine's capacity to tolerate repetitive impact — rather than as something to protect from.
red_flags: sharp, localized, or one-sided pain that persists after the run stops (rather than a symmetrical fatigue 'pump' that clears with rest)
any radiating leg pain, numbness, tingling, or weakness
a discrete injury moment / 'pop' during running rather than gradual cumulative tightening
pain that progressively worsens session to session despite sensible load management
night pain or pain unrelated to the activity
intake_questions: Does the tightness build up gradually during the run and clear with rest, with no specific injury moment?
Is it symmetrical fatigue/ache rather than sharp, one-sided, or radiating pain?
At roughly what distance/duration or intensity does it appear, and is it getting better as your mileage base improves?
Any leg symptoms (numbness, tingling, weakness) at all during or after running?
workaround: Treat as trainable endurance, not an injury to avoid. Build lumbar erector and QL isometric/endurance capacity (timed back-extension holds to neutral, side-plank and front-plank endurance ladders, bird dog, dead bug, loaded carries — farmer's and suitcase — and McGill 'big-3'-style anti-extension/anti-lateral-flexion work) so the trunk tolerates sustained postural load. Develop hip extension/glute strength and running-specific posture so the erectors aren't doing the hips' job. Progress running volume and impact gradually (sensible weekly mileage increase) to expand impact tolerance. Cue a tall, braced, slightly ribs-down posture under fatigue. No movement is contraindicated; if a routing decision is needed, slightly bias trunk-endurance and hip-strength work and avoid spiking impact volume. Re-screen if symptoms change character toward pain, asymmetry, or radiation.

label: Acute non-specific low-back pain (recent flare, recovering)
description: A recent, non-specific low-back pain episode without clear directional preference or radicular signs — diffuse ache, stiffness, and movement guarding, often after an awkward movement or with no clear cause, in the first days-to-weeks of recovery. Functionally most loaded and end-range trunk movements are temporarily irritable and load tolerance is reduced. The evidence-based aim is to avoid catastrophizing and bed rest, stay active within tolerance, and graded-expose the spine back to normal movement and load. Routing keeps everything sub-threshold and neutral early, then systematically rebuilds capacity.
red_flags: saddle (groin/perineal) numbness, or new bowel/bladder dysfunction — possible cauda equina, emergency care now
progressive leg weakness, foot drop, or pain/numbness radiating below the knee
significant trauma, or pain in someone with osteoporosis/long-term steroid use — rule out fracture
fever, unexplained weight loss, history of cancer, or constant unremitting night pain (possible infection/malignancy)
age <20 or >55 at first onset with severe/non-mechanical pain
intake_questions: When did this episode start, and is it improving, plateaued, or worsening day to day?
Is the pain staying in your back, or does it travel into your buttock or leg?
Is there any direction (bending forward vs. leaning back) that clearly eases or worsens it?
Any numbness, tingling, leg weakness, or bladder/bowel changes (any 'yes' here is a stop-and-refer)?
workaround: Reassure and keep moving — avoid bed rest. Stay active within a tolerable range; use gentle non-provocative movement (walking, cat-camel, hip-hinge unloaded, McGill big-3) to reduce guarding. Keep early loading neutral-spine, bilateral, supported, and sub-threshold; temporarily reduce range and load on heavy hinge/squat/loaded-flexion patterns, then progress load step-wise as pain settles and tolerance returns. Once a directional preference emerges (centralizes with extension vs. flexion), route per the corresponding flexion- or extension-intolerant strategy. Rebuild trunk endurance and hip-hinge competency before chasing maximal load. Avoid end-range loaded flexion, ballistic/maximal lifts, and aggressive stretching into pain while acutely irritable. If not steadily improving over ~4-6 weeks, or any red flag appears, refer out.

label: Spondylolisthesis / lumbar segmental instability (diagnosed)
description: A diagnosed structural condition where one vertebra has slipped forward on the one below (spondylolisthesis, often L5-S1 or L4-L5), or a clinically identified segmental-instability presentation. Functionally it is an extension- and shear-sensitive pattern: provoked by lumbar extension and rotation, repetitive end-range loading (common in gymnasts, throwers, divers, cricket fast bowlers), and a feeling of the back 'giving way', catching, or needing to self-stabilize. Routing strongly favors a stiff, braced, neutral spine, anti-movement core control, and avoidance of end-range extension, rotation, and shear; this is the most conservative of the lumbar templates and should generally be cleared/guided by a clinician.
red_flags: any new or progressive leg numbness, tingling, weakness, or foot drop
saddle numbness or bowel/bladder changes — emergency
neurogenic claudication (leg symptoms with standing/walking, eased by sitting) — needs review
a sudden increase in slip symptoms, instability, or pain — requires clinician reassessment before continued loading
this diagnosis generally warrants clinician clearance before progressive loading at all
intake_questions: Has a clinician diagnosed spondylolisthesis or instability, and at what level / grade, and are you cleared to load?
Does arching/extending or rotating your back provoke it, and does bracing into a neutral/slightly-flexed position help?
Do you get a sense of the back 'giving way', catching, or needing to brace to feel stable?
Any leg symptoms (numbness, tingling, weakness) or leg symptoms with walking that ease when you sit?
workaround: Most conservative routing: maintain a stiff, braced, neutral-to-slightly-flexed lumbar spine and emphasize anti-movement trunk control (dead bug, bird dog, plank/side-plank, Pallof, suitcase carry) to stabilize the segment. Strongly avoid end-range lumbar extension and hyperextension (overhead pressing into arch, hyperextension benches, superman/deep cobra), loaded rotation, and high-shear or ballistic spinal loading. Prefer supported, bilateral, neutral-spine pressing and hinging with conservative range and load; favor flexion-biased or neutral positions if the person is extension-sensitive. Develop hip mobility and glute strength so the lumbar segment isn't the relief valve for stiff hips. Build load tolerance slowly and keep technique strict. Because this is a structural diagnosis, default to clinician-guided programming and refer out for any neurological change.

label: Patellofemoral pain syndrome (anterior knee pain / runner's knee)
description: Diffuse pain around or behind the kneecap from how the patella tracks and loads in the trochlear groove. Functionally it is a load-tolerance problem of the patellofemoral joint: pain scales with knee-flexion angle under load (compressive force rises steeply past ~60-90 degrees) and with activities that combine a flexed knee and body weight. Classically aggravated by stairs (especially descending), deep squats, prolonged sitting (the 'theatre sign'), and downhill walking. Not a structural blockage; it is sensitised tissue plus often weak hip-abductors/quads and a tracking issue.
red_flags: true locking or the knee giving way / buckling
significant swelling that fills the joint, especially rapid or after a twist
pain with fever, redness, or warmth (possible joint infection)
inability to bear weight or straighten the knee
pain that is constant, night pain, or unexplained weight loss
intake_questions: Which specific movements set it off most — descending stairs, deep squats, or sitting a long time — and at roughly what knee bend angle does it start?
On a 0-10 scale, what is the pain during your worst aggravating activity, and how long does it linger afterward (minutes, hours, into the next day)?
Is there any swelling, clicking with pain, catching, or a feeling the knee might give out?
Can you do a pain-free partial squat or step-down, and to what depth before pain appears?
workaround: Favor a pain-free range: limit knee flexion to the depth that stays comfortable (often box squats / partial squats / leg press in a shortened range) rather than deep squats, and bias spanish squats and isometric/short-arc quad work which load the quad with less patellofemoral compression. Reduce open-chain leg extension at high flexion angles and through inner-range only if tolerated. Build hip-abductor and glute-med strength (the classic driver) and quad strength progressively. Keep load below the pain threshold (mild pain <=3/10 that settles within 24h is acceptable); avoid plyometrics/running volume spikes and prolonged deep-knee positions early. Substitute deep squats with leg press at limited depth, step-ups to a low box, and hip-dominant work that spares the patellofemoral joint.

label: Meniscus tear / injury
description: Damage to the fibrocartilage shock-absorbers between femur and tibia, from acute twisting on a planted foot or degenerative wear. Functionally it is a problem of loaded rotation and deep compression: pain and catching arise when the knee is loaded in deep flexion and especially when rotated/twisted under load, or pinched at end-range. Degenerative tears often behave like load-sensitive joint pain and respond to exercise; acute mechanical tears can produce true locking. The joint line is typically tender; deep squatting, pivoting, and twisting are the hallmark provokers.
red_flags: true mechanical locking — the knee gets stuck and cannot fully straighten or bend (possible bucket-handle tear needing surgical opinion)
the knee gives way / collapses under you
significant or recurrent joint swelling
inability to bear weight after an acute twisting injury
a locked knee with a springy block to extension — urgent orthopedic referral
intake_questions: Was there a specific twisting or pivoting incident, or did it come on gradually?
Does the knee ever truly lock or catch so you cannot fully straighten it, or does it give way?
Is there swelling, and does deep squatting or twisting on a planted foot reproduce the pain at the joint line?
How deep can you squat or bend before it catches or hurts, and can you walk and bear weight normally?
workaround: Avoid loaded deep flexion and any twisting/pivoting under load early on; train in a controlled mid-range with the foot tracking straight over the knee. Favor leg press and squats to a comfortable partial depth, controlled tempo, no rotation. Bias quad and hamstring strengthening and gradually reintroduce depth as tolerated (degenerative tears respond well to progressive loading). Avoid plyometrics, cutting/pivoting drills, and end-range loaded flexion until pain-free. Substitute deep barbell squats with box squats to a tolerable height, leg press in a limited range, and straight-plane hinge/step work. If true locking occurs, stop and refer out.

label: Patellar / quadriceps tendinopathy (jumper's knee, extensor-mechanism tendon pain)
description: Overuse degeneration/pain of the patellar tendon (below the kneecap) or quadriceps tendon (above it) from accumulated load that outpaced the tendon's capacity. Functionally it is an energy-storage tendon problem: pain is localised to the tendon, worst with explosive and decelerating loads (jumping, landing, sprinting, heavy squats) and with the stretch-shortening cycle. Pain often warms up and returns/worsens after activity. Deep knee flexion under load and ballistic loading are the prime provokers; it responds to progressive tendon loading, not rest alone.
red_flags: sudden pop with inability to straighten the knee or a high-riding/low-riding kneecap (possible tendon rupture — urgent)
marked weakness or inability to do a straight-leg raise / actively extend the knee
pain with significant swelling, warmth, or redness
night pain or rest pain that is severe and unremitting
rapidly worsening pain despite reasonable load management
intake_questions: Exactly where is the pain — just below the kneecap, just above it, or both — and can you point to one spot?
Does it warm up during activity and then ache more later that evening or the next morning?
What loads aggravate it most: jumping/landing, deceleration, or heavy/deep squatting, and at what intensity?
On a 0-10 scale, what is the pain during a single-leg decline squat or step-down, and does it settle within 24 hours?
workaround: Load the tendon, do not just rest it. Start with heavy slow resistance or isometrics (e.g. wall-sit / Spanish squat / leg-extension holds at 30-60s) which reduce pain and build capacity, keeping pain <=3-4/10 during and not worse the next morning (the 24h response rule). Progress to slow-tempo squats and leg press in a tolerable range, then reintroduce speed/plyometrics last and gradually. Reduce — do not eliminate — total jumping/sprinting volume; cut sudden spikes. Bias knee-flexion-angle and tempo to keep the tendon under tension without deep ballistic compression early. Substitute explosive lower-body work with slow-tempo squats/leg press and isometric holds until reactive load is tolerated.

label: Iliotibial band syndrome (lateral knee pain)
description: Pain on the outside of the knee where the iliotibial band crosses the lateral femoral condyle, from compression/irritation of the tissue at around 30 degrees of knee flexion under repetitive load. Functionally an overuse problem of repeated knee flexion-extension cycles (running, especially downhill, and cycling) often with weak hip abductors and poor frontal-plane control. Pain is sharp/burning at the lateral knee, builds with continued activity, and is worst at the foot-strike angle near 30 degrees flexion; deep squatting is usually less of an issue than repetitive mid-range cycling of the knee.
red_flags: lateral knee swelling, locking, or instability (suggests something other than ITB — needs assessment)
pain that does not localise to the lateral femoral condyle or that radiates
night pain or constant rest pain
no improvement after several weeks of appropriate load management and hip strengthening
associated numbness/tingling down the leg (consider nerve or referred source)
intake_questions: Is the pain specifically on the outside of the knee, and does it come on after a predictable distance/time of running or cycling?
Does downhill running or a particular cadence/saddle height make it noticeably worse?
On a 0-10 scale, how bad does it get at its worst, and does it force you to stop the activity?
Have you had recent spikes in running mileage, hill volume, or cycling time?
workaround: Manage load and address the driver: cut the aggravating volume (especially downhill running and high-rep mid-range knee cycling) below the irritation threshold, then rebuild gradually. Bias strengthening of hip abductors / glute-med and frontal-plane control (side-lying abduction, hip-hitch, controlled single-leg work) which is the main fix. Tolerated lower-body strength training (squats, hinges in pain-free range) is generally fine — ITB pain is provoked by repetitive flexion near 30 degrees, not by strength work per se. Avoid foam-rolling-as-cure expectations; the load-management + hip strength path is primary. Substitute downhill/high-volume running temporarily with flatter/shorter runs, cycling adjustments, or hip-focused strength work.

label: Hip femoroacetabular impingement (FAI) / hip impingement
description: Pain at the front/groin of the hip from abnormal contact between the femoral head-neck and the acetabular rim, often with a cam/pincer morphology and sometimes labral involvement. Functionally a deep-flexion and end-range problem: pain (often a deep groin 'C-sign') is provoked by deep hip flexion, flexion combined with adduction and internal rotation, prolonged sitting, and getting into deep squat or hip-hinge end-ranges. The bony block limits available range, so forcing depth pinches the joint. Mid-range loading is usually well tolerated.
red_flags: true hip locking, catching, or giving way (possible unstable labral tear)
deep groin pain with night pain, rest pain, or constant ache
fever, or pain with systemic illness (rule out infection/inflammatory)
progressive loss of range or pain not responding to activity modification
groin pain after significant trauma, or any sudden inability to bear weight
intake_questions: Where exactly is the pain — deep in the groin/front of hip (do you cup the hip with a C-shaped hand)?
Does deep squatting, deep hip bending, or prolonged sitting bring it on, and roughly at what depth does it pinch?
Does the hip ever click painfully, catch, or feel like it gives way?
How much depth (squat / hip flexion) can you reach before the pinch starts, and does it limit daily activities?
workaround: Respect the available range — do not force depth into the pinch. Train squats and hinges to a pain-free depth (box squats / partial range / wider stance / slightly turned-out feet often open the range), and avoid the combined deep flexion + adduction + internal rotation position that provokes impingement. Bias hip-flexor, glute, and deep-rotator strengthening within tolerable range and core/pelvic control. Avoid deep ATG squatting, forced deep stretching into flexion, and high-rep end-range hip flexion early. Substitute deep squats with box/partial squats and trap-bar or wider-stance variations, and deep lunges with shorter-range step-ups. Persistent mechanical catching/locking warrants an orthopedic/physio assessment.

label: Hip-flexor strain (iliopsoas / rectus femoris)
description: A muscle/tendon strain of the front-of-hip flexors (iliopsoas, rectus femoris), from sudden forceful flexion (sprinting, kicking) or overstretch into extension. Functionally a contractile-tissue problem: pain on resisted hip flexion, on stretching the muscle into hip extension, and with explosive flexion. Rectus femoris also crosses the knee, so it is loaded by combined hip-extension + knee-flexion stretch. Pain is localised to the front of the hip/upper thigh; severity ranges from a mild pull to a significant tear.
red_flags: sudden severe pain with a pop and significant weakness or inability to lift the leg (possible high-grade tear/avulsion)
visible large bruise/swelling or a palpable gap/lump in the muscle
in adolescents, acute groin/hip pain after sprinting (possible apophyseal avulsion — image it)
inability to bear weight or walk
groin pain with fever/systemic symptoms, or deep ache unrelated to movement (rule out non-muscular cause)
intake_questions: Was there a specific moment it strained (a sprint, kick, or stretch), and did you feel a pull or pop?
Does resisted lifting of the knee/thigh, or stretching the hip back into extension, reproduce the pain?
On a 0-10 scale, how painful is it, and can you walk, climb stairs, and lift the leg against gravity?
Is there bruising, swelling, or weakness compared with the other side?
workaround: Early on, protect from stretch and explosive flexion — keep within a pain-free range and avoid sprinting, high knees, and deep lunges/stretches that pull the front of the hip. Progress through gentle isometric hip-flexion holds, then mid-range concentric, then controlled eccentric and lengthened loading as it settles (pain <=3/10, no next-day flare). Bias slow, controlled hip-flexor and quad strengthening; rebuild stretch tolerance gradually. Avoid ballistic flexion and aggressive hip-flexor stretching until strong and pain-free through range. Substitute sprint/explosive and deep-lunge work with controlled step-ups and partial-range squats while healing.

label: Adductor / groin strain
description: A strain of the adductor muscles of the inner thigh (commonly adductor longus), from forceful adduction, cutting/change-of-direction, kicking, or overstretch into abduction. Functionally a contractile-tissue problem of the adductor group: pain on resisted adduction (squeezing the legs together), on stretching into abduction (wide stance, side lunges), and with quick lateral/rotational movements. Pain localises to the inner groin/thigh. Chronic cases can blur into groin pain syndromes that need fuller assessment.
red_flags: sudden severe pain with a pop, significant weakness, or a palpable gap (possible high-grade tear/avulsion)
groin pain with a visible/feelable bulge or cough impulse (possible hernia — needs assessment)
groin pain with testicular/abdominal pain, fever, or urinary symptoms (refer out for non-musculoskeletal cause)
inability to bear weight or progressive worsening despite rest
chronic groin pain not improving over weeks (needs differential workup — hip joint, hernia, osteitis pubis)
intake_questions: Was there a specific incident (cutting, kicking, a slip into a wide split) or did it build up gradually?
Does squeezing your legs together (resisted adduction) or a wide stance / side lunge reproduce the inner-groin pain?
On a 0-10 scale, how bad is it, and can you walk, change direction, and bear weight normally?
Is there bruising, swelling, a bulge, or any pain with coughing or sneezing?
workaround: Protect early: avoid wide-stance loading, deep adductor stretch, and cutting/lateral explosive work; keep within a pain-free range. Progress through isometric adduction (ball squeeze) holds — a well-evidenced first step — then mid-range concentric, then controlled eccentric and lengthened adductor loading (e.g. Copenhagen progressions) as tolerance builds, keeping pain low and no next-day flare. Bias narrow-to-moderate stance squats and straight-plane work while healing; rebuild wide-stance and lateral tolerance last. Substitute sumo/wide-stance and lateral/cutting drills with narrower-stance squats and controlled forward step work. Chronic or non-improving groin pain should be assessed for hernia/hip/osteitis pubis.

label: Gluteal / proximal-hamstring tendinopathy (lateral hip or sit-bone pain)
description: Overuse tendon pain at the hip attachments: gluteal tendinopathy at the greater trochanter (lateral hip, the most common cause of 'hip bursitis' pain) or proximal-hamstring tendinopathy at the ischial tuberosity (deep pain right at the sit-bone). Functionally a compressive-tendinopathy problem: both are aggravated by positions that compress the tendon against bone — gluteal by hip adduction (crossing legs, lying on the side, hip-drop) and proximal-hamstring by deep hip flexion (sitting on hard surfaces, deep hinging, sprinting). Pain is local to the attachment, often worse with sustained positions and after loading.
red_flags: sudden pop at the sit-bone with significant weakness/bruising down the back of the thigh (possible proximal-hamstring tendon avulsion — urgent, especially if it bunches up)
buttock pain with leg numbness, tingling, or weakness (possible sciatic/lumbar referral)
unremitting night pain or rest pain, fever, or unexplained weight loss
lateral hip pain with marked weakness or a limp that is not improving
bowel/bladder changes or saddle numbness (urgent — refers out immediately)
intake_questions: Where exactly is the pain — the bony point on the outside of the hip, or deep at the sit-bone where you sit?
Which positions provoke it — lying on that side / crossing legs (gluteal), or sitting on hard surfaces and deep bending (hamstring)?
Does deep hip-hinging, deep stretching, or prolonged sitting make it worse, and does it ache after loading?
On a 0-10 scale, how bad at worst, and is there any numbness, tingling, or weakness running down the leg?
workaround: Reduce compression and load the tendon progressively. Avoid the compressive end-ranges early — for gluteal: avoid hip adduction / hip-drop / crossing legs and side-lying on it; for proximal-hamstring: avoid deep hip flexion, deep hinging, and prolonged sitting on hard surfaces. Start with isometrics (e.g. isometric hip abduction for gluteal, isometric hamstring bridge/hold for hamstring) at low compression, then progress to mid-range strengthening and finally lengthened/end-range loading as tolerated, keeping pain low with no 24h flare. Bias glute-med and hamstring strength built in shortened-to-mid range. Substitute deep stiff-leg/Romanian deadlifts and deep stretching with shorter-range hinges and bridges; avoid stretching into the compressive position (it often worsens tendinopathy).

label: Knee osteoarthritis
description: Age-/wear-related degeneration of knee cartilage with bony change, causing pain, stiffness, and reduced load tolerance. Functionally a joint load-capacity problem: pain and stiffness are worst with sustained or high compressive load, deep flexion, stairs, prolonged standing/walking, and after inactivity (morning stiffness that eases with movement). It is not a contraindication to exercise — progressive strengthening is a first-line treatment — but volume and depth must be titrated to the joint's tolerance, and flares managed. Impact and deep loaded flexion are the main provokers.
red_flags: hot, red, swollen, or fevered knee (possible infection or inflammatory arthritis flare — refer out)
the knee locking or giving way / buckling (possible loose body or mechanical block)
rapidly worsening pain, a large new effusion, or pain at rest/night that is severe
significant deformity or sudden inability to bear weight
calf swelling/pain/warmth (rule out DVT) after reduced activity or surgery
intake_questions: When is it worst — first thing in the morning (and how long does the stiffness last), with stairs/squatting, or after being on your feet a while?
On a 0-10 scale, what is your typical pain with daily activity, and what activities have you had to give up or limit?
Does the knee swell, lock, catch, or give way, and is the pain in one part of the knee or all over?
How far can you walk, and how deep can you bend/squat, before pain limits you?
workaround: Keep moving and strengthen — progressive resistance and aerobic exercise are first-line and reduce pain over time. Train within a comfortable range and depth (partial squats / leg press to tolerance / step-ups to a low box), keep low-impact (cycling, swimming, walking) for aerobic load, and titrate volume to avoid flares — mild pain <=3-4/10 settling within 24h is acceptable. Bias quad, glute, and hamstring strengthening and load progression over time; manage flares with relative rest then return, don't stop training. Avoid high-impact/plyometric and prolonged deep loaded flexion when symptomatic. Substitute deep/high-impact lower-body work with range-limited leg press, low-box step-ups, and low-impact conditioning.

label: Subacromial (subacromial-pain) impingement / bursitis
description: Compression and mechanical irritation of the subacromial structures (supraspinatus tendon, subacromial bursa, long-head biceps) in the space beneath the acromion and coracoacromial arch. Functionally it presents as a 'painful arc' in mid-range elevation (~60-120 degrees) that is worse overhead, with pain on reaching, pressing, and lying on the shoulder. Often driven by scapular control deficits and posterior-capsule tightness rather than a true structural 'pinch'. Modern physiotherapy frames it as subacromial pain syndrome and treats it as a loading and motor-control problem, not something to permanently rest.
red_flags: pain plus weakness so severe the arm cannot be actively lifted to ~90 degrees against gravity (possible full-thickness rotator-cuff tear)
true night pain that consistently wakes from sleep and is unrelieved by position change
trauma onset (fall on outstretched arm or dislocation) with sudden loss of strength
visible deformity, lump, or palpable defect over the cuff/deltoid
fever, hot swollen joint, or systemic illness (rule out septic bursitis/joint)
neurological signs - numbness, pins-and-needles, or weakness radiating down the arm
intake_questions: At roughly what arc of raising the arm does it hurt, and is it worse with the arm overhead versus at shoulder height?
Can you sleep on that side, and does pain wake you at night?
Does it flare with pressing/overhead work specifically, or also with everyday reaching?
On a 0-10 scale, how irritable is it - how much provokes a flare and how long does the flare last?
workaround: Stay below the painful arc and out of end-range overhead. Favor neutral/landmine and incline-to-~30-45-degree pressing over strict vertical overhead, and scapular-plane (thumbs-up, ~30 degrees forward of frontal) raises kept below shoulder height instead of full-range lateral raises. Bias horizontal pulling and serratus/scapular-control work (scapular protraction, wall slides, prone Y/T at low load) to restore the force couple. Use a pain-monitoring rule (work in the 0-3/10 'acceptable' range, settling by next day). Progressively reload range as tolerance returns rather than avoiding overhead forever.

label: Rotator-cuff tendinopathy (supraspinatus / cuff tendinopathy)
description: Overuse degeneration and reactive change of the rotator-cuff tendons (most often supraspinatus), the classic 'tendinitis' though it is usually non-inflammatory tendinopathy. Presents as load-related lateral/deltoid-region shoulder pain that is worst with overhead and abduction tasks and with the eccentric lowering of load; stiffness and ache after activity rather than a sharp catch. It is load-tolerant and responds well to progressive resistance, especially isometric and slow heavy resistance - the goal is graded loading, not rest.
red_flags: sudden weakness or inability to actively lift/hold the arm after a single load or fall (suspect acute tear)
drop-arm sign - cannot lower the abducted arm under control
night pain that consistently disturbs sleep and progressive rest pain
rapidly worsening pain/weakness despite appropriate load management
constitutional symptoms (fever, unexplained weight loss) or a hot, red, swollen joint
intake_questions: Did the pain build up gradually with training volume, or start with a single event?
Which specific movements load it most - overhead pressing, lateral raises, or rotation work?
How does it behave the day after training - settle, stay the same, or worsen (24-hour response)?
Have you noticed any actual loss of strength, or is it pain limiting you rather than weakness?
workaround: Treat as a progressive-loading rehab target, not an avoidance. Start with pain-tolerable isometrics (e.g., external-rotation holds at the side) and build into slow, heavy, full-range resistance as symptoms allow. Keep working sets in an acceptable pain band (0-3/10, settled by next day). Reduce range and load on overhead/abduction provocateurs first - swap strict overhead press for landmine or incline press, full lateral raises for scapular-plane raises below shoulder height. Include cuff-specific external/internal rotation at light load and scapular stabilizers. Manage total weekly volume and avoid abrupt spikes; deload, do not stop.

label: Rotator-cuff tear (partial or full-thickness)
description: A structural defect in one or more cuff tendons, ranging from a partial-thickness fraying to a full-thickness tear with retraction. Functionally distinguished from tendinopathy by true weakness - difficulty initiating or holding abduction/elevation, a positive drop-arm sign with larger tears, and weakness on resisted rotation - alongside pain. Atraumatic degenerative tears are common with age and many are managed conservatively with loading; traumatic full-thickness tears in younger or active people, or any tear with progressive weakness, need surgical evaluation. This template defaults to caution because an undiagnosed or post-acute full-thickness tear is a refer-out, not a self-managed loading problem.
red_flags: inability to actively raise or hold the arm against gravity, or a positive drop-arm sign (full-thickness tear until proven otherwise)
acute traumatic onset (fall, dislocation, sudden load) with immediate weakness
progressive or worsening weakness over days to weeks
significant unremitting night pain
any tear not yet assessed by a clinician where strength is clearly reduced - needs imaging/exam before loading
intake_questions: Has this been confirmed by a clinician or imaging, and is it described as partial or full-thickness?
Can you actively lift the arm overhead and hold it there, or does it drop / give way?
Did it start with a specific trauma, or come on gradually?
Is the limiting factor weakness, pain, or both - and is the weakness getting worse?
workaround: Refer out first for any unconfirmed tear with weakness, any traumatic full-thickness pattern, or progressive weakness - these are not self-loaded. For a clinician-cleared, conservatively-managed (typically partial or small degenerative) tear, load progressively within a pain- and weakness-tolerant range: begin with sub-maximal isometrics and scapular-plane work below shoulder height, avoid end-range overhead and behind-the-neck positions, avoid hanging/dead-hang traction and ballistic/impact loading. Favor supported and machine-guided pressing/rowing over heavy free-weight overhead. Progress only as active strength and control improve; do not chase range or load into weakness.

label: Anterior / multidirectional shoulder instability & subluxation
description: Excessive or symptomatic glenohumeral translation - the humeral head slides too far on the glenoid, causing apprehension, a feeling the shoulder will 'pop out', recurrent subluxation, or frank dislocation. Anterior instability (often post-dislocation, sometimes with a labral/Bankart lesion) is provoked by the abducted-and-externally-rotated 'cocking' position; multidirectional instability (MDI) is often atraumatic, bilateral, hyperlaxity-driven, and provoked in several directions including inferior traction. The functional risk is not pain-on-load but loss of control at end range, so the strategy is to build dynamic stability (cuff + scapular control) while avoiding the provocative end-range positions.
red_flags: an acute dislocation that has not been professionally reduced and assessed (medical emergency)
numbness, tingling, weakness, or cold/pale hand after a dislocation or subluxation (neurovascular compromise - axillary nerve)
recurrent dislocations (the joint comes fully out), which warrant orthopedic/surgical evaluation
a first-time traumatic dislocation, especially under ~25 years (high re-dislocation risk - needs assessment)
instability with a sense of the arm 'dead' or giving way under load
intake_questions: Has the shoulder ever fully dislocated, or does it just feel loose / partially slip (sublux)?
In which arm position does it feel most unstable - arm up-and-back (cocking), overhead, or hanging/loaded down?
Was the onset traumatic, or has it always been loose (and is the other shoulder loose too)?
Do you get an 'apprehension' or guarding feeling at end range even without pain?
workaround: Avoid the provocative end-range positions: keep the abducted-externally-rotated 'cocking' position, deep horizontal-abduction stretch (e.g., deep dumbbell-fly bottom, behind-the-neck press/pulldown), and full-overhead lockout out of the program until control is built. Avoid loaded dead-hangs and inferior traction for MDI. Train in the scapular plane and mid-range, emphasizing rotator-cuff and scapular-stabilizer strength, closed-chain pressing (push-ups, landmine, machine press with a defined stop), and controlled tempo. Reintroduce overhead and rotation range gradually as dynamic control improves. Refer post-dislocation cases for assessment before heavy loading.

label: Acromioclavicular (AC) joint sprain / osteoarthritis
description: Injury or degeneration of the small acromioclavicular joint at the top of the shoulder where the clavicle meets the acromion. A sprain ('separated shoulder') follows a fall onto the point of the shoulder; AC osteoarthritis is wear of the same joint. Functionally it gives pinpoint pain over the top of the shoulder localized to the AC joint, provoked by horizontal adduction across the body (the cross-body / high-cable-fly position), by bench/dip lockout, and by direct pressure. The hallmark is a positive 'cross-body adduction' and 'high-arc' (above ~120 degrees) pain pattern - distinct from the mid-arc impingement pattern.
red_flags: a high-grade separation - obvious step-deformity / prominent bump at the AC joint after trauma (grade III+ needs orthopedic assessment)
severe pain with any arm movement immediately after a fall onto the shoulder
neurovascular symptoms (numbness, weakness, pale/cold hand) after the injury
skin tenting over the clavicle or an open/threatened skin injury (surgical referral)
pain or a mass that is progressive, night-predominant, or with systemic symptoms (rule out other pathology)
intake_questions: Is the pain pinpoint right on top of the shoulder over the AC joint, or more diffuse around the side/front?
Does reaching across your body or a deep fly position specifically light it up?
Did it follow a fall or knock onto the point of the shoulder, or come on gradually as wear?
Is there a visible bump or step at the top of the shoulder compared with the other side?
workaround: Avoid the compressive AC positions: cut deep cross-body / horizontal-adduction work (flat & high cable flyes, deep dumbbell flyes), full bench/dip lockout, full overhead lockout, and end-range cross-body stretches. Bench with a slightly reduced range (stop short of full adduction/lockout) or use a neutral-grip / floor / board-press style, and keep flyes shallow. Favor rowing and mid-range pressing that stays out of cross-body adduction. Keep the bar/load path in front of, not across, the body. Reintroduce range as the joint settles. For confirmed higher-grade separations, refer before loading.

label: Long-head biceps tendinopathy / SLAP (superior labral) lesion
description: Pain arising from the long head of the biceps tendon in the bicipital groove and/or its attachment to the superior labrum (a SLAP lesion - superior labrum anterior-to-posterior). Functionally it gives anterior shoulder pain localized to the front of the joint, provoked by overhead and behind-the-body positions, by loaded elbow flexion/supination (curls, chin-ups), and by deep horizontal-abduction stretch that tensions the anterior structures. SLAP tears in particular dislike the abducted-externally-rotated overhead position and traction/hanging loads. Tendinopathy is loadable and rehab-responsive; a symptomatic SLAP tear with mechanical catching may need orthopedic assessment.
red_flags: a painful 'pop' or tearing sensation at the front of the shoulder with sudden loss of strength (possible biceps tendon rupture - Popeye deformity)
a visible bulge of the biceps muscle belly after a sudden event
mechanical locking, catching, or clunking with overhead/rotation (mechanical SLAP - needs imaging)
instability or apprehension accompanying the anterior pain (combined labral/instability lesion)
progressive weakness or night pain unresponsive to load management
intake_questions: Where exactly is the pain - pinpoint at the front of the shoulder in the bicipital groove, or deeper in the joint?
Does it flare more with overhead/throwing positions, with curls/chin-ups, or with the arm stretched back?
Is there any catching, clicking, or a sense the joint slips with overhead movement?
Did it begin gradually with training, or with a single forceful or traction event?
workaround: Reduce anterior tendon load: avoid behind-the-body and full-overhead positions, deep horizontal-abduction/anterior stretch, and loaded dead-hangs / hanging traction. Scale heavy supinated elbow flexion (barbell curls, weighted chins) toward neutral-grip / supported variants at moderate load, and keep the elbow in front of the body. Press in neutral grip below full overhead (landmine, incline). Build into progressive cuff and scapular work and reintroduce overhead/supinated loading gradually. Refer mechanical-catching or suspected-rupture presentations for assessment before reloading.

label: Adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder)
description: Inflammation and progressive fibrosis/contracture of the glenohumeral joint capsule causing global loss of both active and passive range - the hallmark being restricted passive external rotation that the person cannot move through even with help. It is a self-limiting but slow condition passing through painful 'freezing', stiff 'frozen', and 'thawing' phases over many months to a couple of years, more common in 40-60-year-olds and strongly associated with diabetes and thyroid disease. Functionally it is a hard global ceiling on overhead, rotation, and behind-the-back motion; the limit is capsular range, not strength, so it is treated as a mobility constraint with gentle pain-respecting loading.
red_flags: onset after significant trauma (rule out fracture/dislocation before labeling it capsulitis)
constitutional symptoms - fever, unexplained weight loss, or a history of cancer (rule out sinister cause of a stiff painful shoulder)
rapidly progressive pain with neurological deficit
no diagnosis yet - a globally stiff shoulder should be clinician-confirmed (it mimics OA, posterior dislocation, and cuff pathology)
severe unrelenting pain in the freezing phase that is not settling - warrants medical review for pain management
intake_questions: Which phase are you in - mostly painful with motion (freezing), stiff but less painful (frozen), or regaining motion (thawing)?
Can someone else move your arm into external rotation/overhead, or is it blocked passively too (not just by your own muscles)?
Do you have diabetes or a thyroid condition, or did this come on without any clear injury?
How does pushing into the stiff range feel afterward - tolerable ache that settles, or a flare lasting more than a day?
workaround: Respect the capsular range ceiling - work strictly within available pain-free range and do not force end-range. Keep all pressing, raising, and rotation below the point of capsular block; substitute full overhead and behind-the-back movements with in-range, supported alternatives. Avoid loaded dead-hangs and aggressive end-range stretching that flares the painful phase. Maintain strength of the non-restricted ranges and the rest of the body, use gentle pain-tolerable mobility/pendulum and active-range work, and re-expand range as the 'thawing' phase allows. This is a long-timeline mobility limit, not a quick fix - keep it clinician-guided.

label: Scapular dyskinesis (scapular control deficit)
description: Altered position and motion of the scapula - winging, early/excessive shrug, or loss of upward-rotation rhythm - that disrupts the scapulohumeral force couple and predisposes to or accompanies impingement, cuff, and instability problems. It is usually a motor-control and stabilizer-endurance issue (weak/poorly-timed serratus anterior and lower trapezius, often with a tight/overactive upper trap and pec minor) rather than a pain pathology in itself. Functionally it shows as a shoulder that fatigues, aches, or pinches under overhead/pressing volume and a visibly 'off' shoulder-blade rhythm. It is a correctable control deficit, so the strategy is to rebuild scapular stability and timing rather than to avoid load.
red_flags: frank scapular winging that appeared suddenly or after trauma/viral illness (possible long-thoracic or spinal-accessory nerve palsy - needs neurological assessment)
winging with numbness, weakness, or pain radiating down the arm (nerve involvement)
progressive, unexplained scapular muscle wasting
dyskinesis accompanied by true instability/dislocation or by clear cuff weakness (treat the primary pathology)
no improvement in control or worsening symptoms despite appropriate scapular rehab
intake_questions: Has anyone pointed out that your shoulder blade wings out or sits differently, or do you mainly notice fatigue/aching with overhead volume?
Did this start gradually with training, or suddenly / after an illness or injury (which would change the picture)?
Is there any numbness, tingling, or weakness, or is it purely a control/endurance issue?
Does pressing and overhead work fatigue or pinch as the sets accumulate, and does it improve when you slow down and focus on the shoulder blade?
workaround: Treat as a control-and-endurance rebuild, not an avoidance. Prioritize scapular-stabilizer work - serratus-anterior (scapular protraction, push-up-plus, wall slides, landmine press) and lower-trapezius (prone Y/T, face pulls, controlled rows) at moderate load with good rhythm. Keep overhead and lateral-raise volume in a range where scapular control holds (reduce range/load before form breaks; stop the set when the blade rhythm fails rather than grinding reps). Address the typical tight upper-trap/pec-minor side with mobility. Reintroduce full overhead pressing as control and endurance improve. Refer sudden/traumatic or neurological winging for assessment before loading.

label: Lateral Epicondylitis (Tennis Elbow)
description: Degenerative tendinopathy of the common wrist-extensor origin (chiefly ECRB) at the lateral epicondyle of the elbow. Pain and weakness on resisted wrist extension and gripping; the loaded forearm extensors pull on a fraying tendon. Functionally it limits anything that combines a hard grip with wrist extension or static forearm tension, and any pronated/reverse-curl loading of the extensor mass.
red_flags: pain radiating down the forearm with numbness/tingling or hand weakness (suggests radial-tunnel or cervical nerve involvement, not simple tendinopathy)
night pain at rest or pain unrelated to load
visible swelling, warmth, or locking/catching of the elbow (suggests joint pathology, not tendon)
sudden loss of grip strength or a palpable gap (possible tendon rupture)
no improvement after 6-8 weeks of appropriate load management
intake_questions: Does it hurt to grip and lift a coffee mug, a kettle, or shake hands, or only under heavy gym load?
On a 0-10 scale, how irritable is it: does pain settle within minutes after a provoking activity, or linger for hours/into the next day?
Is the pain pinpoint over the bony bump on the outside of the elbow, or does it spread down the forearm?
Can you currently do a pain-free wrist extension or reverse curl with light load?
workaround: Favor isometric and slow heavy-eccentric wrist-extensor loading as rehab (typically therapeutic, not contraindicated) kept below a tolerable pain threshold (roughly =3/10 that settles quickly). Reduce crush-grip demand: thinner bar or neutral-grip handles, switch free weights to machine/cable variants, and use lifting straps to cut grip tension on pulls. Favor supinated and neutral elbow positions over pronated/reverse-curl loading, and load through cables/machines that let the wrist stay neutral. Avoid maximal grip, sustained static holds, dead-hangs, and ballistic/impact wrist actions during the irritable phase. Build tolerance progressively.

label: Medial Epicondylitis (Golfer's Elbow)
description: Degenerative tendinopathy of the common wrist-flexor/pronator origin at the medial epicondyle of the elbow. Pain on resisted wrist flexion, forearm pronation, and gripping; the flexor mass that drives a hard grip pulls on an irritated tendon. Functionally it limits heavy gripping, wrist-curl/flexor loading, pronated curls, and any pull where the grip is the limiting tension.
red_flags: numbness, tingling, or weakness in the ring and little fingers (suggests ulnar-nerve involvement at the cubital tunnel, not just tendinopathy)
night pain at rest or pain unrelated to activity
elbow locking, catching, or swelling
sudden sharp loss of grip or wrist-flexion strength (possible tendon rupture)
symptoms persisting or worsening beyond 6-8 weeks of load management
intake_questions: Where exactly is the pain: the bony bump on the inside of the elbow, or more diffuse?
Do you get any pins-and-needles or numbness in the ring or little finger?
How irritable is it: does pain settle within minutes of stopping a grip task, or persist for hours?
Can you currently grip and do a light wrist curl or pronated curl without provoking it?
workaround: Favor isometric and heavy-slow-eccentric wrist-flexor/pronator loading as therapeutic rehab, kept under a tolerable pain ceiling (~=3/10, settles fast). Cut crush-grip demand with straps on pulls, neutral/thinner handles, and machine or cable variants that remove the need to squeeze. Prefer neutral-wrist, supinated/neutral elbow loading; deload heavy wrist-flexion (wrist curls), pronated curls, and maximal grip during flare-ups. Avoid sustained holds, dead-hangs, pinch grips, and ballistic/impact wrist actions while irritable. Progress load gradually as the daily-pain response improves.

label: Distal Biceps Tendinopathy
description: Overuse tendinopathy of the distal biceps tendon at its insertion on the radial tuberosity, felt deep in the front of the elbow. Provoked by resisted elbow flexion combined with forearm supination (the biceps' two jobs), and by heavy supinated pulls/curls and end-range elbow extension that stretches a loaded tendon. Functionally limits supinated curling, chin-ups/underhand pulls, and heavy stretch at the bottom of a curl.
red_flags: sudden 'pop' with sharp pain, bruising, and a bunched-up ('Popeye') deformity of the biceps (suggests acute distal tendon rupture - urgent surgical referral, often time-sensitive)
marked weakness of supination or elbow flexion after an acute event
rapidly worsening swelling or pain at rest
no progress after 6-8 weeks of structured tendon loading
intake_questions: Was there a single sudden tearing/popping event, or did the ache come on gradually over weeks?
Is the pain deep in the front of the elbow (the crease), and worse when you curl with the palm turning up?
How does the bottom of a curl - the fully straightened, stretched position - feel under light load?
How irritable is it: brief soreness after lifting, or a deep ache that lingers into the next day?
workaround: If any sudden-rupture picture exists, refer out before loading. Otherwise treat as load-management tendinopathy: favor isometric holds and controlled heavy-slow loading of elbow flexion in a mid-range, pain monitored (=3/10, settles quickly). Temporarily favor neutral/hammer and pronated elbow flexion over fully supinated curling, and reduce end-range stretch at the bottom of curls (limit ROM or use a preacher/cable that loads the mid-range). Use straps on heavy pulls so grip isn't the limiter, and avoid ballistic curling and dead-hangs while irritable. Reintroduce full-supination and full-stretch loading progressively.

label: Wrist Extensor / Flexor Tendinopathy & Tenosynovitis
description: Overuse irritation of the wrist-extensor or wrist-flexor tendons (and their synovial sheaths) along the forearm and dorsal/volar wrist - distinct from epicondylitis in that the pain sits at the wrist/forearm rather than the elbow origin. Tenosynovitis adds sheath swelling and sometimes crepitus. Provoked by repeated wrist flexion/extension under load, end-range wrist positions, and sustained gripping. Functionally limits wrist-curl loading, loaded wrist extension (front-rack position, push-ups), and any movement forcing the wrist to end range under load.
red_flags: audible/palpable creaking or crepitus with marked swelling along the tendon (suggests acute tenosynovitis needing rest/medical review)
numbness or tingling in the hand (consider nerve compression rather than tendon)
redness, heat, and swelling out of proportion to load (rule out infection/inflammatory arthritis)
wrist gives way or a specific spot is acutely tender after a fall (rule out fracture, e.g. scaphoid)
no improvement after 4-6 weeks of relative rest and load management
intake_questions: Is the pain at the wrist/forearm itself, or up at the elbow?
Does any position - bending the wrist back (push-up, front-rack) or forward - reproduce it sharply?
Is there any swelling, creaking, or crepitus when you move the wrist?
How quickly does it settle after a provoking session - minutes, hours, or the next day?
workaround: Favor neutral-wrist loading: use wrist wraps for support, push-up handles/dumbbells to keep the wrist straight, and machine/cable or strap-assisted variants that avoid forcing the wrist to end range under load. Reduce loaded wrist flexion/extension volume; substitute the front-rack/loaded-extension positions with neutral-grip or machine equivalents (e.g. machine press over barbell front squat hold). Begin tendon loading with pain-limited isometrics, progress to controlled eccentrics. Avoid ballistic and impact wrist actions and sustained maximal grip while irritable. If crepitus/sheath swelling is present, bias toward relative rest first.

label: De Quervain's Tenosynovitis
description: Stenosing tenosynovitis of the first dorsal compartment (APL and EPB tendons) at the thumb-side of the wrist. Pain on thumb movement and ulnar deviation of the wrist; classically reproduced by the Finkelstein maneuver (thumb tucked, wrist bent toward the little finger). Functionally limits pinch grip, thumb-loaded gripping, and any wrist ulnar/radial deviation under load - common with thumb-around barbell grips, kettlebell work, and pinch holds.
red_flags: significant swelling, redness, or a fluid-filled lump at the thumb-side wrist
numbness/tingling over the back of the hand or thumb (consider superficial radial nerve irritation)
symptoms after a fall or direct trauma (rule out scaphoid/radial-styloid fracture)
locking or triggering of the thumb
no improvement after 4-6 weeks of relative rest, splinting, and load management - escalate for possible injection/medical review
intake_questions: Is the pain on the thumb-side of the wrist, and worse when you move or load the thumb (lifting, gripping, wringing)?
Does tucking the thumb into the fist and bending the wrist toward the little finger sharply reproduce it?
Any recent new repetitive activity (new baby, new grip work, repetitive thumb texting/tooling)?
How irritable is it - provoked only by hard pinch/thumb load, or by everyday tasks?
workaround: Offload the thumb and first compartment: avoid thumb-around ('thumb-wrap') barbell grips, pinch grips, and ulnar-deviation-loaded carries during the irritable phase. Use a thumb-spica style splint outside training as advised, neutral-wrist machine/cable variants, lifting straps or wrist cuffs so the thumb/grip isn't the limiter. Keep the wrist neutral (avoid forced radial/ulnar deviation under load). Reintroduce thumb-loaded gripping and pinch work progressively once Finkelstein-type provocation calms. Splinting plus relative rest is first-line; refer out if it stays irritable.

label: TFCC Injury (Triangular Fibrocartilage Complex)
description: Injury or degeneration of the triangular fibrocartilage complex on the ulnar (little-finger) side of the wrist - the cartilage/ligament cushion stabilizing the distal radioulnar joint. Pain on the pinky-side of the wrist with loaded rotation (pronation/supination), ulnar deviation, and axial compression through the hand (push-ups, front-rack, weight-bearing on the hand). Functionally limits loaded wrist rotation, weight-bearing on the palm, and gripping with rotation under load.
red_flags: a clunk, click, or instability sensation with forearm rotation (suggests DRUJ instability - needs imaging/specialist review)
ulnar-wrist pain after a fall on an outstretched hand or a forced rotation injury (rule out fracture and acute tear)
marked swelling, locking, or sharp catching
significant loss of forearm rotation or grip strength
no improvement after 4-6 weeks of relative rest and bracing - escalate to hand specialist (some tears need imaging/surgical input)
intake_questions: Is the pain specifically on the little-finger side of the wrist, and worse when you twist/rotate the forearm under load or push through the palm?
Was there a specific injury (fall on the hand, a twist) or did it build gradually?
Do you get any clicking, clunking, or a feeling the wrist might give way when you rotate it?
Which provokes it most: pushing through the hand (push-ups, front-rack), or rotating under load?
workaround: Offload the ulnar wrist and DRUJ: avoid palm-weight-bearing (push-ups, dips on the hand, front-rack holds) and loaded forearm rotation while irritable - substitute push-up-on-handles/dumbbells or machine presses that keep the wrist neutral and unloaded in rotation. Use an ulnar-side wrist brace/wrap for support, neutral-grip handles, and straps so grip-with-rotation isn't required. Favor fixed-path machine and cable work over free rotation. Keep axial load off the palm. Reintroduce rotation and weight-bearing progressively; refer out if instability/clunking is present.

label: Carpal Tunnel Syndrome
description: Compression of the median nerve at the wrist, producing numbness, tingling, and sometimes weakness in the thumb, index, middle, and half the ring finger. Provoked or worsened by sustained wrist flexion/extension at end range, prolonged gripping, and pressure on the carpal tunnel (e.g. leaning on the heel of the hand, sustained wrist-extended push-ups). This is a nerve constraint, not a tendon one - the goal is to keep the wrist neutral and minimize sustained pressure on the nerve.
red_flags: constant (not intermittent) numbness, or visible wasting/weakness of the thumb-base muscles (suggests advanced nerve damage - needs prompt specialist review)
symptoms spreading above the wrist or into the neck/shoulder (consider cervical or more proximal nerve cause)
rapidly worsening weakness or dropping objects
numbness affecting the little finger too (suggests a different nerve - ulnar - and a different problem)
no improvement with splinting/load management, or progressive symptoms - refer for nerve studies
intake_questions: Which fingers go numb or tingly - thumb/index/middle (median) or the little finger (different nerve)?
Do symptoms wake you at night or come on with sustained gripping/wrist positions?
Is the numbness intermittent (comes and goes) or constant, and is there any hand weakness or clumsiness?
Does a neutral wrist position relieve it, and does end-range bending bring it on?
workaround: Keep the wrist neutral under load: use wrist wraps, push-up handles/dumbbells, and neutral-grip machine/cable variants that avoid sustained end-range flexion/extension. Reduce sustained maximal gripping and long static holds (carries, dead-hangs) that pressurize the tunnel; use straps to cut grip duration/intensity. Encourage a neutral wrist at rest and a night splint as advised. Avoid loading into the positions that reproduce numbness. Because this is a nerve compression, monitor symptoms closely - if numbness becomes constant or weakness appears, stop and refer out rather than pushing through.

label: Finger-Flexor / Grip Overuse & Jammed Finger
description: Overuse or acute irritation of the finger flexors (FDP/FDS), pulley/tendon structures, or a single jammed/sprained finger joint - the crush-grip-mediated type seen with heavy hanging, thick-bar work, and weight hanging off one digit (e.g. a dumbbell bell loading the little-finger side). Pain on hard gripping, hanging, and pinch; a jammed finger adds localized joint pain, swelling, and pain on end-range flexion. Functionally limits crush-grip, hangs, pinch holds, and any movement where load transmits through the affected digit.
red_flags: inability to actively bend the finger or a felt 'pop' at the fingertip (suggests flexor tendon avulsion / 'jersey finger' - urgent hand-surgery referral)
obvious deformity, inability to straighten/bend the joint, or instability after a jam (rule out fracture/dislocation/ligament rupture)
rapidly worsening swelling, redness, or a fixed/locked joint
numbness in the finger (consider digital nerve injury)
a jammed finger not improving after 1-2 weeks, or any locked/triggering finger - get it assessed
intake_questions: Is it a gradual grip ache across the hand/forearm, or a specific jammed/sprained single finger from an event?
Which loads provoke it most - hanging, heavy crush-grip, thick bar, pinch, or a bell hanging off the little-finger side of a dumbbell?
Can you fully bend and straighten the finger, and is there swelling, locking, or a 'pop' in its history?
How irritable is it - sore only during/after heavy grip, or aching at rest and into the next day?
workaround: Route load off the affected grip/digit: cable wrist cuffs are best (they remove hand grip entirely); lifting straps and figure-8s help pulls but do NOT spare a crush-grip or a bell hanging off the pinky side - use cuffs or machine/fixed-handle variants for those. Prefer machine-loaded and cable substitutes over free dumbbells that hang off one digit; avoid dead-hangs, thick-bar, pinch, and maximal crush-grip while irritable. For a jammed/sprained finger, protect with buddy-taping, avoid end-range flexion under load, and keep load distributed across the whole hand. Reintroduce grip-intensive work progressively once pain-free under light load; refer out for any locking, deformity, or inability to bend the finger.

label: Achilles tendinopathy
description: Load-related degeneration/pain of the Achilles tendon (mid-portion or insertional), felt at the back of the heel/lower calf. Classically stiff and painful for the first steps in the morning and when the tendon is loaded under speed or stretch; warms up with light activity but flares the day after heavy plantarflexion or impact. It is a tendon CAPACITY problem, not an inflammation to rest away — the tendon tolerates heavy slow load but hates sudden spikes, bounce, and compression at end-range dorsiflexion (especially the insertional type).
red_flags: sudden sharp pop/snap with a feeling of being kicked in the calf, then inability to push off or rise on the toes (suspect Achilles rupture - urgent)
a palpable gap or dent in the tendon
calf swelling with redness, warmth, and disproportionate pain (rule out DVT)
pain that is severe, constant, and unrelated to load, or worsening night pain
numbness/tingling or foot drop
intake_questions: Where exactly is the pain - mid-tendon (2-6 cm above the heel) or right at the heel bone insertion? (insertional types hate full dorsiflexion stretch and deep heel-drops)
On a 0-10 scale, what's your pain during and the morning AFTER a hard set of calf raises? Does it settle to baseline within 24 hours?
Can you do a single-leg heel raise, and a small hop, without sharp pain?
How long has it been bothering you, and is it trending better, same, or worse over the last few weeks?
workaround: Treat it as a capacity problem: keep loading but make it heavy-and-slow, not bouncy. Favor controlled isometric and slow-tempo plantarflexion (seated and standing calf raise, leg press calf press) over plyometrics, jumping, running, and skipping rope. Pain up to ~3-4/10 during the set that settles by next morning is acceptable; sharper or next-day-worse means back off load. For INSERTIONAL pain, limit the bottom range - avoid dropping the heel into deep dorsiflexion (raise off a step), do flat-ground or partial-ROM raises. Build calf volume on machines/seated work; avoid loaded carries and explosive split squats during a flare. Progress load gradually over weeks; never spike volume.

label: Lateral ankle sprain / chronic ankle instability
description: Stretch or tear of the lateral ankle ligaments (classically ATFL) from the foot rolling inward (inversion), or the residual 'giving way' instability that persists after repeated sprains. Acutely painful, swollen, and bruised over the outside of the ankle; chronically it feels unstable, weak, or untrustworthy on uneven ground, single-leg work, and lateral movement. The provoking demand is uncontrolled inversion/eversion and any unstable single-leg loading; pain-free straight-plane loading is usually fine.
red_flags: unable to bear weight (take 4 steps) right after the injury, or bony tenderness over the ankle/foot bones - Ottawa Ankle Rules positive, screen for fracture
gross deformity or the joint looks dislocated
rapid massive swelling, severe bruising, or the ankle feels 'loose'/dislocating (possible complete ligament tear)
numbness, coldness, or loss of pulse in the foot
no improvement at all after a week or two of sensible management
intake_questions: Is this an acute sprain (recent, swollen, bruised) or long-standing instability (repeated rolls, 'gives way')?
Can you bear full weight and walk without a limp, and was that true right after the injury?
Does it give way or feel unstable on single-leg work, stairs, or uneven ground?
How many times have you sprained this ankle before?
workaround: Acutely, respect tissue healing - avoid forced inversion/eversion and unstable single-leg loading; keep training the rest of the body. For loading the lower body, favor BILATERAL, fixed-path, flat-foot work (leg press, hack squat, machine-supported squat, seated calf) over free-standing single-leg, deep lunges, lateral bounds, and balance-board work until pain and confidence return. Reintroduce single-leg and direction-change work gradually once pain-free and stable, ideally alongside dedicated balance/proprioception rehab (a hallmark of preventing re-sprain). Lace bracing or taping can let straight-plane loading continue. Avoid impact/ballistic work and end-range ankle stress during a flare.

label: Plantar fasciitis / plantar heel pain
description: Overload of the plantar fascia at its attachment on the heel bone, felt as sharp pain under the heel/arch. The signature is intense pain with the FIRST steps in the morning or after sitting, which eases as you warm up but returns after prolonged standing, walking, or loaded standing work. It is irritated by sustained weight-bearing, impact, and heavy standing calf/toe-off load rather than by any seated or upper-body movement.
red_flags: heel pain following a fall or jump with focal bony tenderness (rule out calcaneal stress fracture)
numbness, tingling, or burning into the sole/heel (possible nerve entrapment, e.g. tarsal tunnel - refer out)
bilateral heel pain with other joint pain, swelling, or morning stiffness lasting >30-60 min (screen for inflammatory arthropathy)
redness, warmth, swelling, or fever (possible infection)
no response to several weeks of sensible load management and calf/fascia loading
intake_questions: How bad is the pain on the very first steps in the morning, 0-10, and how long until it eases?
Does prolonged standing or walking bring it back later in the day?
Is the pain pinpoint under the heel, or more diffuse through the arch?
Any recent spike in standing time, walking/running volume, or change in footwear?
workaround: Manage standing/weight-bearing load and keep training. Favor SEATED and supported lower-body work (leg press, leg extension, leg curl, seated calf raise) and reduce time under load on the feet - swap long loaded carries and prolonged standing-station circuits for seated alternatives during a flare.
