Progressive calf and plantar-fascia loading (high-load slow heel raises, often with the toes propped into extension) is the evidence-backed driver of recovery; introduce it gradually. Supportive shoes/orthotics and reducing impact (running, jumping, rope) help. Pain that settles to baseline by the next morning is the loading guide.

label: Shin splints (medial tibial stress syndrome)
description: Exercise-induced pain along the inner border of the shin (lower-to-mid tibia) from repetitive impact loading - the bone-tissue and surrounding fascia overloaded by a spike in running, jumping, or high-impact volume. Classically a diffuse ache over several centimeters of the shinbone that hurts at the start of impact activity, may ease as you warm up early on, and worsens with continued pounding. It is an impact/volume overload, NOT aggravated by seated or non-impact strength work.
red_flags: pain that has narrowed to one PINPOINT spot on the bone, hurts at rest or at night, and worsens session over session (suspect a tibial STRESS FRACTURE - stop impact and get imaged)
pain on hopping on the affected leg, or pain reproduced by tuning-fork/percussion over a focal point
severe swelling, tight/numb/cold lower leg with pain out of proportion (rule out exertional compartment syndrome - urgent)
numbness or weakness in the foot
no improvement despite reducing impact load over several weeks
intake_questions: Is the pain spread along a span of the shin (typical) or pinpoint on one spot (concerning for stress fracture)?
Does it hurt at rest or at night, or only with impact activity?
Did your running, jumping, or impact volume jump recently?
Can you hop on that leg without sharp focal pain?
workaround: This is a load-management problem: deload impact, keep strength training. Favor NON-IMPACT lower-body strength and conditioning (leg press, leg curl, leg extension, machine work, cycling, swimming) over running, jumping, and plyometrics until symptoms calm. Reintroduce impact gradually and progressively (do not return to prior running volume at once). Address contributing factors - footwear, surface, calf strength, and especially the volume spike that triggered it. Calf and tibialis loading helps build capacity. If pain localizes to one bony point or persists at rest, treat as a stress fracture until proven otherwise and refer out.

label: Cervical (neck) strain / mechanical neck pain
description: Strain of the neck muscles and supporting soft tissue, producing localized neck pain, stiffness, and reduced range of motion, often with referral into the upper traps or base of the skull. Symptoms stay in the neck/shoulder-girdle (no arm radiation). Aggravated by sustained end-range neck positions, overhead loading that demands neck extension, heavy bracing/valsalva that lets the neck crane, and prolonged loaded flexion (e.g. looking down). It is a movement/posture-sensitive soft-tissue problem that generally settles with gentle motion and avoiding the provoking positions.
red_flags: pain, numbness, tingling, or weakness radiating down the arm or into the hand (suspect nerve root involvement - see radiculopathy)
neck pain after trauma/whiplash, or with midline bony tenderness (rule out fracture/instability before loading)
headache with fever, neck rigidity, or feeling generally unwell (rule out meningitis)
dizziness, fainting, double vision, slurred speech, or facial/limb numbness (possible vascular/neurological cause)
any clumsiness in the hands, gait/balance problems, or bladder/bowel changes (possible spinal cord involvement - urgent)
intake_questions: Is the pain only in the neck/shoulder area, or does it travel into the arm or hand?
Which movements set it off - looking up (extension), looking down (flexion), turning, or holding a position for a while?
Did it start after an injury/whiplash, or come on gradually with posture/load?
Any numbness, tingling, weakness, dizziness, or headache?
workaround: Keep the neck in a neutral, supported position and avoid the provoking end-ranges. Favor CHEST-SUPPORTED and machine-guided work that doesn't load the neck (chest-supported row, machine press, supported rows over barbell overhead pressing). Temporarily swap strict overhead pressing and behind-the-neck movements for landmine/incline or neutral-grip presses; swap heavy loaded carries and shrugs that let the neck crane for lighter, well-braced versions. Avoid dead-hangs that traction an irritable neck, prolonged loaded flexion, and breath-holding (valsalva) on heavy sets - exhale and keep a packed neutral neck. Gentle range-of-motion and not freezing the neck up speeds recovery.

label: Cervical radiculopathy (pinched nerve root)
description: Compression or irritation of a cervical nerve root (disc, foraminal narrowing), producing pain, numbness, tingling, or weakness that radiates from the neck down a specific path into the shoulder, arm, and hand. Classically worsened by extending and/or rotating the head toward the painful side (which closes the foramen) and by axial loading; sometimes EASED by overhead arm positioning. Overhead pressing, end-range neck extension, axial compression, and traction-type hangs can all provoke or worsen the radiating symptoms. This carries a genuine neurological component and a lower threshold to refer out.
red_flags: progressive or significant arm/hand WEAKNESS, or muscle wasting (motor deficit - refer promptly)
symptoms in BOTH arms, or any leg involvement, gait/balance problems, hand clumsiness, or bladder/bowel changes (suspect cord compression/myelopathy - urgent)
rapidly worsening or unrelenting pain, or severe night pain
fever, unexplained weight loss, or history of cancer with new neck/arm symptoms
onset after significant trauma (rule out fracture/instability before any loading)
intake_questions: Where exactly do the symptoms travel - which part of the arm/hand, and is it pain, numbness, tingling, or weakness?
Does looking up or turning your head toward the bad side reproduce the arm symptoms? Does anything (e.g. hand on head) relieve them?
Is there any weakness, dropping things, or clumsiness in the hand?
Are symptoms in one arm only, and are they getting better, staying the same, or getting worse?
workaround: Default to caution and avoid anything that loads the neck into extension or compresses the nerve root. ELIMINATE overhead pressing and behind-the-neck work during an active flare; favor chest-supported, neutral-spine, machine-guided pulling and pressing that keeps the neck packed and neutral (chest-supported row, neutral-grip / landmine press, machine work). Avoid axial-loaded barbell work that compresses the spine (heavy back squats, overhead carries), avoid dead-hangs and weight-hanging that traction an irritable nerve, and avoid valsalva/breath-holding which spikes intradiscal/intrathecal pressure - keep loads moderate and breathe. Because this is neurological, any motor weakness, two-arm/leg signs, or progression should be referred out before continuing to load. Train pain-free regions in the meantime.

label: TMJ dysfunction / jaw clenching under load
description: Temporomandibular joint dysfunction - jaw pain, clicking, or limited/painful mouth opening, often tied to clenching or bruxism. It matters for lifting because hard sets - especially heavy grip, maximal effort, and breath-held (valsalva) braced lifts - reflexively trigger jaw clenching, which loads and aggravates the TMJ. It is not a movement-pattern problem so much as a behavioral one (the unconscious clench under strain), so the fix is a cue/equipment intervention rather than a substitution.
red_flags: the jaw locks open or closed and won't move (acute locked TMJ)
jaw pain with facial swelling, fever, or trouble swallowing/breathing (refer out)
jaw or left-arm pain/tightness brought on by exertion that could be cardiac (clenching can mask referred cardiac pain - do not dismiss exertional jaw pain)
progressive limitation of mouth opening or persistent severe jaw/ear pain
numbness or facial weakness
intake_questions: Do you notice yourself clenching your jaw, or get jaw/temple/ear pain, on heavy or maximal sets?
Is there clicking, popping, or locking, or any limit to how wide you can open?
Does it flare more with breath-held grinder sets (heavy squats/deadlifts) or with hard grip work?
Have you been diagnosed with TMJ/bruxism or use a night guard already?
workaround: Mostly a cueing fix - no exercise needs to be removed, just loaded more mindfully. Primary cue: consciously UNCLENCH the jaw and keep the tongue relaxed on heavy sets; bite a soft mouthguard/bite splint on maximal or valsalva-braced lifts to offload the joint. Prefer a controlled, exhale-paced brace over a maximal teeth-gritted breath-hold; cap valsalva to short, necessary efforts and avoid grinding-style grinders. Keep grip-intensive holds (heavy carries, dead-hangs) shorter or use straps so the whole-body clench reflex is smaller. If symptomatic, lower intensity slightly and avoid ballistic/jarring work; persistent or locking jaw warrants a dental/TMJ referral.

label: Systemic load/valsalva caution (uncontrolled hypertension, hernia, recent surgery, pregnancy)
description: A cluster of whole-body conditions where the issue is not a single joint but the SYSTEMIC stress of heavy loading - chiefly the intra-abdominal/intrathoracic pressure spike of the valsalva-braced maximal lift, axial compression, and hard trunk bracing. Covers: uncontrolled or poorly-controlled hypertension (heavy valsalva spikes blood pressure sharply), abdominal/inguinal hernia or hernia risk (bracing strains the abdominal wall and can enlarge/incarcerate a hernia), recent surgery (healing tissue/incisions can't take bracing or axial load yet), and pregnancy (the supine position late on, hard valsalva, falls/impact, and over-stretch all warrant modification). Each of these warrants medical clearance rather than self-managed loading - they are refer-out conditions.
red_flags: chest pain/pressure, severe shortness of breath, palpitations, fainting, severe headache, or vision changes during or after exertion (stop immediately - emergency)
a bulge in the groin/abdomen that becomes painful, hard, red, or can't be pushed back, with nausea/vomiting (possible incarcerated/strangulated hernia - urgent)
pain, bleeding, gaping, or discharge at a surgical site, or loading before surgeon clearance
in pregnancy: vaginal bleeding, fluid leak, severe abdominal/pelvic pain, painful contractions, dizziness/fainting, calf swelling, or any 'stop activity' instruction from the clinician
blood pressure that is very high at rest or symptomatic
intake_questions: Which applies - high blood pressure, a hernia (or hernia history), recent surgery, or pregnancy - and have you been medically cleared to lift?
For blood pressure: is it controlled and what does your clinician say about heavy/breath-held lifting?
For hernia/post-surgery: any bulge, pain on bracing, or lifting restriction from your surgeon, and how long since the operation?
For pregnancy: which trimester, any complications, and what activity guidance has your provider given?
workaround: Default to medical clearance first - this is a refer-out cluster, not a self-managed gym tweak. Across all of these, MINIMIZE the valsalva/axial-pressure spike: keep loads sub-maximal, use a controlled exhale-through-the-effort breathing pattern instead of a held maximal brace, and favor machine-supported, well-supported, lower-pressure work over heavy free-weight grinders. Specifically: for hypertension, avoid maximal breath-held efforts and overhead/inverted positions; for hernia, avoid hard bracing, heavy hinging, and big intra-abdominal pressure spikes; post-surgery, follow the surgeon's load timeline and avoid loading the healing region; in pregnancy, modify per trimester (avoid prolonged supine work later on, avoid valsalva, impact, fall-risk, and deep over-stretch), keep effort moderate, and follow the obstetric provider's guidance. When in doubt, refer out and train only what's been cleared.
